title: Uterine Fibroids: Treat Symptoms, Location, and Reproductive Goals
bottomLine: Leiomyomas are benign uterine smooth-muscle tumours managed according to bleeding, bulk symptoms, anemia, location, fertility/pregnancy goals and patient preference—not imaging size alone. Confirm that bleeding/pain is actually attributable to fibroids and escalate rapidly growing postmenopausal or otherwise atypical masses for specialist evaluation.
recognize: Heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary/bowel bulk symptoms, infertility or pregnancy complications can occur depending on number and location.
Many fibroids are incidental and require no treatment.
differentiate: Adenomyosis, endometriosis, pregnancy, endometrial pathology and ovarian/adnexal masses can mimic pain/bleeding.
Postmenopausal bleeding should not be attributed to known fibroids without endometrial evaluation.
assessment: Characterize bleeding, pressure/pain, anemia symptoms, pregnancy possibility, fertility goals, age/menopause status and prior imaging/procedures.
workup: Use CBC/ferritin when heavy bleeding suggests iron deficiency and pelvic ultrasound to define uterine anatomy when findings will alter care.
Use endometrial sampling based on age/risk/bleeding pattern rather than fibroid presence alone.
management: Observation is appropriate for asymptomatic disease.

Medical bleeding control, GnRH-modulating strategies, uterine artery embolization, myomectomy or hysterectomy are selected according to symptoms, anatomy and reproductive goals through current gynecology pathways.
medicationSafety: Hormonal therapy requires the same estrogen/progestin contraindication review as other indications.
GnRH therapies and procedural options have bone, hypoestrogenic, fertility and pregnancy implications that require individualized counselling.
redFlags: Acute severe pain/possible degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated lesion
Rapidly enlarging or atypical pelvic mass
counselling: Explain that fibroid size does not automatically determine treatment and that preserving fertility or avoiding uterine surgery can change the options.
followUp: Track bleeding, hemoglobin/iron status, bulk symptoms and reproductive plans; repeat imaging only when symptoms or treatment planning justify it.
examTrap: Sending every fibroid to surgery based on size while ignoring that the patient is asymptomatic—or attributing postmenopausal bleeding to fibroids without evaluating the endometrium.
oneLinePearl: Fibroid treatment follows symptoms, location and goals—not centimetres alone.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada uterine leiomyoma/abnormal bleeding practice resources

title: Endometrial Cancer: Postmenopausal Bleeding Is Cancer Until Evaluated
bottomLine: Postmenopausal bleeding and abnormal bleeding in a patient with significant endometrial-cancer risk require timely endometrial evaluation. Screening asymptomatic average-risk patients is not the same as diagnosing symptoms; ultrasound can stratify selected cases, but tissue diagnosis is required when the pathway indicates it.
recognize: Postmenopausal bleeding is the classic presenting symptom; abnormal heavy/irregular bleeding can also occur before menopause.
Risk rises with prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure, obesity, chronic anovulation/PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome and age.
differentiate: Atrophy, polyps, fibroids and medication-related bleeding are common but do not eliminate cancer risk.
A normal cervical screening result does not evaluate the endometrium.
assessment: Clarify menopausal status, bleeding amount/pattern, pregnancy possibility when relevant, hormone/tamoxifen use, PCOS/anovulation, BMI/metabolic risk, Lynch/family history and anemia symptoms.
workup: Use transvaginal ultrasound and/or endometrial sampling according to the current symptomatic bleeding pathway and individual risk.
Persistent/recurrent postmenopausal bleeding requires further evaluation even after an initially reassuring test when the clinical pathway indicates it.
management: Refer abnormal endometrial pathology or persistent high-risk bleeding to gynecology/gynecologic oncology promptly.
Treat hemodynamic bleeding/anemia in parallel rather than waiting for outpatient cancer workup.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe repeated empiric progestin/hormonal therapy for unexplained high-risk bleeding without ensuring appropriate endometrial assessment.
redFlags: Persistent/recurrent bleeding despite initial reassuring evaluation
counselling: Explain that most bleeding causes are benign, but timely evaluation matters because endometrial cancer often presents early with bleeding.
followUp: Track pathology and specialty referral to definitive diagnosis; do not let bleeding resolution cancel indicated evaluation.
examTrap: Reassuring a postmenopausal patient because bleeding stopped after one episode or because cervical screening is up to date.
oneLinePearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is a diagnostic pathway, not a watch-and-wait symptom.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada abnormal uterine bleeding resources

title: Ovarian Cancer: Persistent Symptom Pattern, Risk, and the Limits of Screening
bottomLine: There is no effective routine population screening strategy for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic average-risk patients. Persistent new bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary symptoms or an adnexal mass require diagnostic assessment, with hereditary-risk patients routed to genetics/specialty care rather than serial CA-125 screening alone.
recognize: Symptoms are often nonspecific but become concerning when new, persistent and frequent—especially after menopause.
BRCA-related hereditary cancer and Lynch/family history can materially raise risk.
differentiate: IBS, urinary disease, fibroids and benign ovarian cysts can mimic symptoms.
CA-125 can rise in benign conditions and can be normal in malignancy; it is not a stand-alone screening or diagnostic test.
assessment: Assess symptom duration/frequency, weight loss, abdominal distension, menopausal status, family/personal breast-ovarian-colorectal cancer history, prior imaging and pregnancy possibility when relevant.
workup: Use pelvic/transvaginal ultrasound as appropriate for an adnexal mass and integrate morphology, menopausal status and validated risk assessment.
Tumour markers support selected diagnostic/specialist pathways but do not replace imaging and clinical risk.
management: Refer suspicious adnexal masses to gynecology/gynecologic oncology before non-oncologic surgery when malignancy risk is substantial.
Offer genetic counselling/testing pathways when hereditary risk criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly prescribe symptom treatments or order serial CA-125 in place of diagnostic evaluation for a persistent concerning syndrome.
counselling: Explain why routine screening is not recommended for average-risk asymptomatic people but persistent symptoms still deserve evaluation.
followUp: Track imaging/referral/genetics to diagnostic closure; persistent symptoms require reassessment even after an initially benign explanation.
examTrap: Ordering annual CA-125 and ultrasound as routine screening in an asymptomatic average-risk patient—or dismissing persistent new bloating because symptoms are nonspecific.
oneLinePearl: Ovarian cancer is not a population-screening disease; it is a persistent-symptom and adnexal-risk diagnostic problem.

title: Bone Health Across Reproductive Aging: Prevent Fractures Before the First One
bottomLine: Bone-health prevention is risk-based across the lifespan: identify premature estrogen loss, glucocorticoid exposure, low-trauma fracture, low weight/nutrition risk and other secondary causes, then use exercise/falls/nutrition plus bone-density or pharmacologic pathways when fracture risk warrants them. Do not wait for an older-age screening milestone when a younger patient has major risk.
recognize: Menopause accelerates bone loss; POI/early menopause extends estrogen deficiency over more years.
A fragility fracture is a major risk signal even if a prior BMD was not in the osteoporosis range.
differentiate: Osteoporosis diagnosis/risk is not based on calcium level and BMD is not the only fracture-risk determinant.
Pregnancy/lactation-associated bone loss, eating disorders, celiac disease, hyperparathyroidism and medications can produce secondary bone disease.
assessment: Assess fracture history, falls, menopause/POI, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, nutrition, exercise, family history, body weight and secondary disease/medications.
workup: Use BMD and fracture-risk assessment according to age/risk and investigate secondary causes when clinical features warrant it.
Avoid routine broad bone-marker testing without a management question.
management: Ensure adequate dietary calcium/nutrition and vitamin D where needed, weight-bearing/resistance exercise, falls prevention and smoking/alcohol risk reduction.
Use pharmacotherapy for sufficiently high fracture risk with drug selection based on renal function, fracture site/risk, age, pregnancy potential and long-term sequencing.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonates/denosumab and other therapies require indication-specific renal/calcium/dental/reproductive review.
Denosumab discontinuation requires a transition plan to avoid rebound bone loss/fractures.
redFlags: Severe hypocalcemia risk before antiresorptive therapy
Rapid bone loss with systemic disease
counselling: Explain fracture prevention rather than presenting BMD as a score to chase; discuss exercise and medication duration/sequence realistically.
followUp: Reassess fracture risk, adherence and medication strategy at clinically meaningful intervals rather than ordering frequent BMD without a decision attached.
examTrap: Waiting until standard older-age screening because a 38-year-old with POI and chronic glucocorticoid exposure is 'too young' for bone-risk assessment.
oneLinePearl: Bone prevention follows fracture risk and estrogen/medication history, not age alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Menopause Society menopause and osteoporosis resources

title: Sexual Dysfunction: Desire, Arousal, Orgasm, Pain, Context, and Consent
bottomLine: Sexual concerns require patient-defined distress and a biopsychosocial assessment. Clarify whether the main problem is desire, arousal, orgasm, pain/penetration, genitourinary symptoms, medication effect, relationship/context or trauma/coercion; treat the contributors and do not medicalize low desire that is not distressing to the patient.
recognize: Pain can arise from genitourinary syndrome of menopause, infection, vulvodynia, pelvic-floor hypertonicity, endometriosis or dermatologic disease.
SSRIs/SNRIs and other medications commonly affect desire, arousal and orgasm.
differentiate: Asexuality or lower desire without distress is not a disorder.
Pelvic-floor overactivity and fear/pain cycles require different therapy from low estrogen alone.
IPV, reproductive coercion or sexual trauma can present as pain or avoidance and requires safety-centred care.
assessment: Ask permission, use inclusive language and assess the patient's goals, onset/context, pain location, arousal/orgasm, menopausal/postpartum symptoms, medications, mood, sleep, relationship factors and safety/consent.
workup: Use focused pelvic/dermatologic/infection or endocrine testing only when symptoms indicate it; routine hormone panels do not diagnose most sexual dysfunction.
management: Treat identified causes: medication adjustment, vaginal moisturizers/lubricants or local estrogen when appropriate, pelvic-floor physiotherapy, psychotherapy/sex therapy, pain/endometriosis/vulvar treatment or relationship/safety supports.
Use pharmacologic treatments for specific diagnosed disorders only after contraindication and goal review.
medicationSafety: Do not stop effective psychiatric medication abruptly because of sexual adverse effects; weigh relapse risk and alternatives.
Systemic versus local hormone choices have different risk profiles and indications.
redFlags: Pain with fever or pregnancy concern
counselling: Normalize discussion, affirm consent and autonomy, and explain that sexual function is influenced by health, medications, life stage and context rather than one hormone level.
followUp: Track the patient-defined outcome—comfort, desire, function or distress—rather than a clinician-defined frequency target.
examTrap: Ordering testosterone/estrogen panels for every patient reporting low desire before asking whether it causes distress, reviewing medications, pain, menopause and relationship/safety context.
oneLinePearl: Sexual health treatment starts with the patient's distress, goals and context—not a lab panel.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada sexual-health and pelvic-health practice resources
